label: NOISE

turns.user_message: We're finally pulling the trigger on replacing our appointment scheduling software. We've been on Dentrix version 11.0.44 since 2019, and we want to migrate to Curve Dental's cloud platform. Our office has 3 providers and about 4,200 active patient records.
turns.assistant_message: That's a solid upgrade path — moving from Dentrix 11.0.44 to Curve Dental's cloud platform is a common transition for small multi-provider practices. With 3 providers and 4,200 active patient records, you'll likely fall into Curve's mid-tier 'Growth' plan, which is priced per provider rather than per record. It's worth confirming with your Curve rep whether your Dentrix data export will require the XML or the HL7 format, since that affects how long the migration validation step takes.

turns.user_message: Our Curve rep confirmed we'll use the XML export path, and she said the data validation window is 14 business days. She also said our go-live date is locked in for March 3, 2025, so we need to have the legacy system fully decommissioned by February 14, 2025 to give the team enough lead time.
turns.assistant_message: Good, having those dates locked down is critical. That means your Dentrix 11.0.44 decommission deadline is February 14, 2025, your XML data validation window runs for 14 business days after that export is submitted, and your Curve go-live is March 3, 2025. Make sure you complete a full Dentrix backup — ideally to an encrypted external drive — before you initiate the export, since Dentrix 11.0.44 does not support post-export rollback within the same installation. Your Curve rep can walk you through the XML schema checklist to ensure all 4,200 patient records map cleanly.

turns.user_message: Completely different situation — we got a notice that our building's fire suppression system is due for its annual inspection. Do you know what's typically involved in that?
turns.assistant_message: Annual fire suppression inspections for commercial buildings generally follow NFPA 25, which is the Standard for the Inspection, Testing, and Maintenance of Water-Based Fire Protection Systems. A certified inspector will check sprinkler heads for corrosion or paint overspray, test the main drain and inspector's test valve, verify that the control valve is fully open and properly supervised, and review the system's pressure readings. You'll also need to make sure the inspection report is kept on file for at least five years, as most local fire marshals require documentation going back that far.

turns.user_message: The inspector mentioned our sprinkler heads are the old fusible-link type and some may be from the original 1987 installation. Is that a problem?
turns.assistant_message: Yes, that's worth taking seriously. NFPA 25 requires that representative samples of sprinkler heads be sent to a recognized laboratory for testing once they reach 50 years of age, but it also recommends replacement when heads show signs of corrosion, loading, or paint — regardless of age. Heads from a 1987 installation are now 37–38 years old, so you're not at the mandatory 50-year sample-testing threshold yet, but an inspector who flags them as visibly degraded can still require replacement. Replacing fusible-link heads with modern quick-response heads is often a good idea anyway, since quick-response heads activate faster and can reduce water damage.

turns.user_message: The inspector also said we need a backflow preventer test. Our plumber says the device is a Watts 007M2 reduced-pressure zone assembly. How often does that need to be tested?
turns.assistant_message: The Watts 007M2 is a reduced-pressure zone (RPZ) backflow preventer, and those are generally required to be tested annually by a certified backflow tester — not just inspected, but functionally tested with a differential pressure gauge. Most municipal water authorities enforce this under their cross-connection control programs, and they typically require the test report to be submitted to the utility within 30 days of the test date. The 007M2 has two independently operating check valves and a differential relief valve, and the tester will verify that each check valve holds at least 1.0 psi differential and that the relief valve opens correctly. Keep the test records; utilities can discontinue water service for noncompliance.

turns.user_message: Our plumber also noticed the building's water heater is a Bradford White RE350S6-1NCWW and said it's 11 years old. Should we be thinking about replacing it?
turns.assistant_message: The Bradford White RE350S6-1NCWW is a 50-gallon, 240-volt electric residential-style water heater, and Bradford White's published average service life for that line is 8 to 12 years. At 11 years old, yours is within that range but on the back end of it, so planning for replacement in the next 12 to 18 months is prudent rather than waiting for a failure. Signs to watch for include rust-colored water, a popping or rumbling sound during heating cycles (indicating sediment buildup), or water pooling near the base. If you do replace it, commercial-grade units like the Bradford White M-I-50S6DS are better suited for the demand profile of a medical or dental office.

turns.user_message: While the plumber was here he pointed out that our dental unit waterlines are overdue for their monthly shock treatment. We use Sterisil tablets — what's the protocol?
turns.assistant_message: Sterisil tablet shock treatments are typically done by dissolving one tablet per 750 mL of water in the bottle reservoir, then running the solution through all handpiece and syringe lines for 10 minutes, followed by a clean-water flush until the residual chlorine reading drops below 0.5 ppm as measured with a colorimetric test strip. The CDC's Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings recommend that dental unit waterlines meet the drinking water standard of ≤500 CFU/mL of heterotrophic bacteria, and routine monthly shocking with Sterisil is one of the validated methods to maintain that threshold. You should also document each treatment date and your post-flush CFU or chlorine readings in a waterline maintenance log for accreditation or OSHA compliance purposes.

turns.user_message: Speaking of compliance, our office manager wants to know if we need to renew our OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens training this year. Our last training was on April 10, 2024.
turns.assistant_message: Yes, OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) requires annual retraining for all employees with occupational exposure, so if the last training was April 10, 2024, the renewal deadline is April 10, 2025. The training must cover the exposure control plan, the epidemiology and symptoms of bloodborne diseases, transmission routes, use of PPE, hepatitis B vaccination information, and post-exposure evaluation procedures — and it must be provided during working hours at no cost to employees. You'll need to retain training records, including employee names, training dates, and a summary of the material covered, for at least three years under 29 CFR 1910.1020.

turns.user_message: Our exposure control plan hasn't been updated since January 2022. Is that going to be a problem?
turns.assistant_message: Potentially, yes — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(c)(1)(iv) requires that the written exposure control plan be reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever tasks or procedures affecting occupational exposure are added or changed. A plan last updated in January 2022 is now more than three years old, which would be a clear citation if OSHA conducted an inspection. You should update it to reflect any staffing changes, new procedures, or updated engineering controls since 2022, and document the review date on the plan itself. It's also good practice to have employees sign an acknowledgment that they've received the updated plan.

turns.user_message: We also need to figure out our sharps container disposal. We use a Stericycle mail-back service — how does that work for a small dental office?
turns.assistant_message: Stericycle's mail-back program for small quantity generators typically works by sending you a pre-approved, DOT-compliant container — usually a 1-gallon or 2.2-gallon sharps container — along with a prepaid shipping label and a return box that meets 49 CFR Part 173 requirements for Category B biological substances. Once the container is two-thirds full (never overfill), you seal it, place it in the return box, affix the prepaid label, and drop it at a UPS or FedEx authorized location. Stericycle provides a certificate of destruction for each shipment, which you should retain for at least three years to satisfy your state's medical waste tracking requirements. For a three-provider dental office, a quarterly pickup cycle is typical, but that depends on your procedure volume.

turns.user_message: Our autoclave is a Midmark M11 and it's been making a clicking sound during the pressure-build phase. Any idea what that could be?
turns.assistant_message: A clicking sound during the pressure-build phase on a Midmark M11 is often associated with the solenoid valve cycling more frequently than normal, which can indicate a small water leak in the chamber seal or a partially obstructed steam line. The M11's service manual (Midmark document 003-1505-00) identifies the door gasket and the chamber drain valve as the two most common sources of pressure inconsistency in that unit. I'd recommend running a Bowie-Dick test cycle first to see if the steam penetration is still adequate, and if it fails or the clicking persists, contacting Midmark's technical support at 1-800-643-6275 before your next sterilization load. Continuing to use the autoclave without diagnosis risks a failed sterilization cycle that could compromise patient safety.

turns.user_message: We run spore tests on the autoclave every Monday. Our last failed spore test was on November 4, 2024. What's the required response protocol?
turns.assistant_message: A failed biological indicator (spore test) on a steam autoclave triggers a specific response under CDC guidelines and most state dental board rules. You must immediately take the autoclave out of service, quarantine all loads processed since the last passing test (in your case, everything sterilized after the prior passing Monday's run), and attempt to contact patients if any instruments from those loads were used in invasive procedures — your state dental board will specify the notification threshold. The autoclave should be inspected and recalibrated before it's returned to service, and you must document the failure, the corrective action taken, and the results of three consecutive passing spore tests before resuming routine use. Keep those records for a minimum of three years.

turns.user_message: Our dental assistant handles all the sterilization logs. She mentioned the office hasn't been tracking instrument cycle counts — is that required?
turns.assistant_message: Instrument cycle count tracking isn't universally mandated by federal regulation, but it is required or strongly recommended by several state dental boards and by AAMI ST79, the industry's primary sterilization guidance document for healthcare facilities. The practical concern is that repeated autoclaving degrades instrument integrity — dental burs, for instance, are typically rated for a maximum of 5 to 10 autoclave cycles by most manufacturers before their cutting efficiency drops and micro-fracture risk rises. If your malpractice carrier or a future accreditation survey asks for instrument lifecycle records and you don't have them, that could create liability exposure. Starting a simple log now — instrument type, purchase date, cycle count — is a low-cost way to close that gap.

turns.user_message: Our office is also thinking about adding a cone beam CT scanner. We're looking at the Planmeca ProMax 3D Mid. What's the radiation dose like compared to a standard panoramic?
turns.assistant_message: The Planmeca ProMax 3D Mid has several field-of-view options, and effective dose varies significantly with FOV and resolution settings. For a small FOV (roughly 4×4 cm) at standard resolution, published effective dose estimates typically fall in the range of 18 to 50 microsieverts, depending on protocol. A standard digital panoramic on a modern unit delivers approximately 14 to 24 microsieverts effective dose, so a small-FOV CBCT is in a broadly comparable range, while a large FOV (e.g., 23×26 cm) can climb to 100–200 microsieverts. The American Academy of Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology recommends applying ALARA principles and selecting the smallest FOV and lowest resolution consistent with the diagnostic task.

turns.user_message: For the CBCT, do we need a separate radiation safety officer, or does our existing dental radiography license cover it?
turns.assistant_message: Requirements vary by state, but in most jurisdictions your existing dental radiography license and facility registration cover intraoral and panoramic X-ray equipment but do not automatically extend to CBCT units, which are classified as advanced imaging devices. Many states require a separate facility registration amendment and proof that the operating dentist has completed a CBCT-specific training course — the American Academy of Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology offers a recognized 8-hour course that satisfies most state requirements. Designation of a Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) is typically required when a facility operates equipment above a certain output threshold; CBCT units often cross that threshold, so you'd need to check your state dental board and radiation control program rules specifically. Penalties for operating unregistered advanced imaging equipment can include fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation day in states with strict enforcement.

turns.user_message: Our building lease is up for renewal in August 2025. The landlord wants to raise the rent from $4,200 per month to $5,100 per month. Is that a reasonable increase for dental office space?
turns.assistant_message: A jump from $4,200 to $5,100 per month represents about a 21.4% increase, which is above the typical annual commercial lease escalation of 3–5% for established tenants in most markets. That said, dental office space commands a premium over general commercial space because of the infrastructure requirements — plumbing for multiple operatories, electrical capacity for compressors and autoclaves, lead-lined walls if you have X-ray rooms — so landlords often justify higher rates for build-out value. I'd recommend pulling comparable dental office lease rates per square foot in your market (a commercial real estate broker with healthcare experience can run comps), and negotiating a longer term — say, 5 or 7 years — in exchange for a lower escalation rate or a tenant improvement allowance. Make sure any renewal agreement includes a cap on future annual increases, typically 3% or CPI, whichever is lower.

turns.user_message: The lease also has a clause saying we're responsible for HVAC maintenance. Our current HVAC unit is a Carrier 50XC series rooftop unit. What does a standard maintenance contract for that cover?
turns.assistant_message: A standard commercial maintenance contract for a Carrier 50XC series rooftop unit typically includes quarterly inspections covering filter replacement (usually 2-inch MERV-8 filters on that unit), coil cleaning, belt and bearing inspection, refrigerant pressure checks, and thermostat calibration. Most contracts also include a semi-annual comprehensive service that checks the heat exchanger for cracks, tests the economizer damper operation, and verifies that the unit's electrical connections are torqued to spec. The 50XC uses R-410A refrigerant, and any contractor handling refrigerant must hold an EPA Section 608 certification. Expect a full-coverage maintenance contract for a rooftop unit that size to run $800 to $1,400 per year depending on your region and whether parts are included.

turns.user_message: We've been having trouble with uneven cooling in the operatories. Two rooms are fine but the third runs about 5°F warmer. What typically causes that?
turns.assistant_message: A 5°F differential between operatories on the same HVAC zone is most commonly caused by one of three things: an unbalanced duct system where the damper serving that branch is partially closed or has drifted out of position, a supply register that's undersized or obstructed by a ceiling tile or furniture, or duct leakage between the main trunk and that room's branch. A certified HVAC technician can perform a simple air balancing test using a flow hood (also called an air capture hood) to measure actual CFM at each register and compare it to the design specification — the design spec for dental operatories is typically 0.15 to 0.20 CFM per square foot of floor area. If the duct system has never been balanced since the build-out, that's the most likely culprit and it's a relatively inexpensive fix.

turns.user_message: One of our hygienists mentioned the air quality in the office might be a concern with all the aerosols from ultrasonic scalers. Are there specific standards for that?
turns.assistant_message: Yes — the CDC's guidance on dental healthcare settings, particularly the 2020 interim recommendations issued in response to aerosol concerns, recommends enhanced ventilation for operatories where aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs) are performed, including ultrasonic scaling. ASHRAE Standard 170-2021, which applies to healthcare facilities, specifies a minimum of 12 total air changes per hour (ACH) for dental treatment rooms, with at least 3 of those being outdoor air changes. High-volume evacuators (HVEs) placed within 1 cm of the ultrasonic tip are the primary source control measure and can reduce aerosol contamination by up to 90% according to published studies. Portable HEPA air purifiers rated at a CADR sufficient for the room volume can supplement fixed ventilation but don't substitute for meeting the ASHRAE 170 ACH requirement.

turns.user_message: We're also looking at adding nitrous oxide sedation to one of our operatories. What scavenging system requirements apply?
turns.assistant_message: OSHA and NIOSH both set limits on nitrous oxide exposure: NIOSH recommends a ceiling of 25 ppm time-weighted average for dental workers, and OSHA's general duty clause is used to enforce that standard in dental settings. A compliant scavenging system for a dental operatory must include a nasal hood with a scavenging mask connected to a high-volume vacuum line flowing at least 45 liters per minute, and the system must be vented directly to the exterior of the building — not into the building's return air plenum. The operatory should also be tested with a real-time infrared nitrous oxide monitor at least annually to verify that ambient levels stay below the 25 ppm threshold during procedures. NIOSH publication number 94-100 is the reference document most dental boards and inspectors use when evaluating compliance.

turns.user_message: Our front desk uses a credit card terminal that's been flagging PCI DSS compliance issues. Our processor is Heartland Payment Systems and the terminal model is a Verifone VX520. What's the most common compliance gap for small offices?
turns.assistant_message: For small practices using a Verifone VX520 through Heartland, the most common PCI DSS compliance gap is running an outdated terminal firmware version that doesn't support TLS 1.2 or higher — PCI DSS version 3.2.1 (and its successor, PCI DSS v4.0, which became the mandatory standard on March 31, 2024) explicitly prohibits the use of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 for cardholder data transmission. The VX520 must be on firmware version 22.01.01 or later to support TLS 1.2; anything older is out of compliance. The second most common gap is failing to complete the annual Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) — for card-present small merchants, SAQ B-IP is the applicable form. Heartland's merchant portal should have your SAQ status and can flag whether your terminal firmware is current.

turns.user_message: We also store some patient payment information in a spreadsheet on an office computer. Is that a problem under PCI DSS?
turns.assistant_message: Yes, that's a significant PCI DSS violation. Storing full primary account numbers (PANs), CVV codes, or magnetic stripe data in any unencrypted format — including a spreadsheet — is prohibited under PCI DSS Requirement 3, regardless of whether the file is password-protected or on a local drive. Even storing only the last four digits of a card number alongside a patient name and expiration date in a spreadsheet creates a data minimization issue. You should immediately identify what card data is in that spreadsheet, delete any prohibited data elements, and document the deletion. Going forward, use Heartland's tokenization service, which replaces card data with a non-sensitive token that can be used for recurring charges without storing actual card numbers on your systems.

turns.user_message: Our office manager also wants to know if we need cyber liability insurance. We have a general business policy through State Farm but she's not sure if that covers data breaches.
turns.assistant_message: Standard commercial general liability (CGL) policies, including those from State Farm, typically do not cover first-party data breach costs — things like forensic investigation, patient notification, credit monitoring services, or regulatory fines under HIPAA. Those costs fall under a separate cyber liability policy, which is distinct from your CGL. For a three-provider dental office with around 4,000–5,000 patient records, a standalone cyber liability policy with $1 million per-occurrence coverage typically costs $1,200 to $2,500 annually depending on your security controls and claims history. Given that the average cost of a healthcare data breach in the U.S. was $10.93 million in 2023 according to the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report, the premium is modest relative to the exposure. Ask your State Farm agent specifically about their CyberFirst product or request quotes from specialty insurers like Beazley or Coalition.

turns.user_message: Our HIPAA Security Risk Assessment is also overdue. The last one was completed on June 15, 2022. How often is that required?
turns.assistant_message: The HIPAA Security Rule at 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1) requires covered entities to conduct a security risk assessment (SRA) on a regular basis — HHS guidance specifies this should be at least annually or whenever significant operational, environmental, or technological changes occur. A last-completed date of June 15, 2022 means you're well past the annual mark and have likely had multiple triggering changes (new staff, software updates, equipment changes) that independently require a fresh assessment. The SRA must evaluate the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all electronic protected health information (ePHI) your practice creates, receives, maintains, or transmits. HHS's free SRA Tool (available at healthit.gov) is an acceptable framework for small practices, and you should document the completed assessment and any corrective action plan in writing.

turns.user_message: We have a part-time IT contractor who manages our server. He mentioned our server is running Windows Server 2012 R2. Is that still supported?
turns.assistant_message: No — Microsoft ended Extended Support for Windows Server 2012 R2 on October 14, 2023. After that date, Microsoft no longer issues security patches for the operating system, which means any new vulnerabilities discovered after that date remain unpatched and exploitable. Running ePHI on an unsupported operating system is a direct HIPAA Security Rule violation because it fails to implement required technical safeguards under 45 CFR 164.312. Your options are to migrate to Windows Server 2022, which has mainstream support through 2026 and extended support through 2031, or to enroll in Microsoft's Extended Security Updates (ESU) program, which provides limited patches at increasing annual cost — but ESU is meant as a short-term bridge, not a permanent solution. Your IT contractor should treat this as an urgent remediation item.

turns.user_message: We've also been thinking about switching our phone system to a VoIP solution. We currently use a Panasonic KX-NS700 PBX. What should we know about transitioning?
turns.assistant_message: The Panasonic KX-NS700 is a hybrid IP-PBX, so it already supports SIP trunking, which makes migrating to a cloud VoIP provider relatively straightforward compared to transitioning from a purely analog system. Key considerations include porting your existing phone numbers to the new provider — number porting typically takes 2 to 4 weeks and must be initiated before you cancel your existing service to avoid losing the numbers. For a dental office, you'll want to confirm that your chosen VoIP provider supports a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (BAA), since voicemails may contain ePHI; RingCentral and 8x8 both offer BAAs, while many consumer-grade VoIP services do not. Also verify that your internet connection has sufficient upload bandwidth — a reliable VoIP call requires about 100 Kbps per concurrent call, and you'll want headroom above that.

turns.user_message: One of our dentists wants to start offering Invisalign. Do we need any special certification or equipment to get started?
turns.assistant_message: To become an Invisalign provider, a dentist must complete Align Technology's online doctor education course, which is available through the Invisalign Doctor Site and takes approximately 4 to 6 hours. There's no separate state licensing requirement for Invisalign specifically — it's covered under the dentist's existing dental license — but Align Technology requires completion of their training before you can submit cases. On the equipment side, an iTero Element intraoral scanner is strongly recommended (and in practice nearly required) for efficient case submission, though PVS impressions are technically still accepted. Pricing for an iTero Element 2 typically starts around $20,000 to $22,000 for purchase, or it can be leased; Align Technology sometimes offers promotional financing tied to case volume commitments. Your first 10 cases are classified as Invisalign First or Comprehensive Tier 1 and are priced at a reduced lab fee to support new providers.

turns.user_message: We've been getting a lot of patient complaints about wait times. Our average chair wait is about 22 minutes after the scheduled appointment time. What's considered acceptable?
turns.assistant_message: Industry benchmarks from the Dental Group Practice Association and various patient satisfaction surveys generally place acceptable wait time at 10 minutes or less from the scheduled appointment time to being seated in the operatory. A 22-minute average is more than double that benchmark and is likely contributing to negative online reviews and patient attrition. Common root causes include overbooking the schedule by using average procedure times rather than 90th-percentile times, inadequate hygiene-to-operatory ratios, or a bottleneck at the front desk check-in process. A useful diagnostic step is to track wait time by provider and by appointment type for 30 days — you'll often find that the problem is concentrated in one provider's schedule or in a specific procedure type like new patient exams, which routinely run long.

turns.user_message: Our office manager wants to implement a patient satisfaction survey. She's looking at using SurveyMonkey — is that HIPAA compliant?
turns.assistant_message: SurveyMonkey's standard (free and lower-tier paid) plans are not HIPAA compliant and should not be used to collect any information that could identify a patient in connection with their health condition or treatment. SurveyMonkey does offer a HIPAA-compliant tier — specifically, their Enterprise plan — which includes a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), but it's priced for larger organizations and may be cost-prohibitive for a small dental office. More practical alternatives for small practices include Birdeye, Solutionreach, or NPS tools built into your practice management software, many of which include BAAs as part of their standard dental office pricing. If your surveys will only ask generic questions with no patient identifiers (no name, DOB, treatment type, or appointment date), the HIPAA concern diminishes, but you'd lose most of the actionable data.

turns.user_message: We're also considering adding a dental membership plan for uninsured patients. What's the typical structure for those?
turns.assistant_message: In-house dental membership plans typically offer patients an annual fee in exchange for a defined set of included services plus a discount on additional procedures. A common structure for a general dentistry practice is an annual membership of $199 to $299 per adult that includes two prophylaxis cleanings, one comprehensive exam, one set of bitewing X-rays, and one emergency exam per year, plus a 15–20% discount on all other procedures. State regulations vary significantly — some states classify these plans as insurance products requiring licensure, while others exempt them under specific carve-outs for direct primary care or discount plans; you'll want to confirm your state's position with a healthcare attorney before launching. Platforms like BoomCloud or Membersy can handle the billing and administrative infrastructure for a monthly fee of around $99 to $199, which is generally more efficient than managing it manually.

turns.user_message: Our receptionist mentioned that several patients have been asking about teeth whitening options. Do we need any special FDA clearance to offer in-office whitening?
turns.assistant_message: Dental bleaching products used in professional in-office settings — typically containing 25% to 40% hydrogen peroxide — are regulated by the FDA as medical devices or as cosmetic products depending on their specific formulation and claims. Products marketed for professional dental use with bleaching concentrations above 10% hydrogen peroxide are generally regulated as Class II medical devices and must have 510(k) clearance; established products like Opalescence Boost (40% hydrogen peroxide) and Philips Zoom WhiteSpeed carry that clearance. As a licensed dentist, you don't need a separate FDA clearance to use cleared products — you just need to purchase and use products that themselves have appropriate clearance and to follow their labeled instructions. Take-home whitening trays you fabricate in-office using custom impressions fall under the practice of dentistry and don't require separate FDA registration.

turns.user_message: We're planning a staff meeting next week and want to cover emergency protocols. Do we need an AED and is there required training?
turns.assistant_message: Most state dental practice acts require dental offices to have an automated external defibrillator (AED) on-site, and the ADA recommends it as a standard of care regardless of state mandate. The AED must be registered with your local EMS system in most jurisdictions, and the registration is typically renewed annually. For training, the American Heart Association's Basic Life Support (BLS) for Healthcare Providers course is the standard for dental staff; it covers CPR for adults, children, and infants, AED use, and relief of airway obstruction, and certification is valid for two years. Most state dental boards require at least one BLS-certified staff member to be present whenever the office is open and patients are being treated, and some require all clinical staff to be certified.

turns.user_message: Our dentist wants to know what emergency drugs we're required to keep on hand. We're in Texas — does the Texas State Board of Dental Examiners have a specific list?
turns.assistant_message: Yes — the Texas State Board of Dental Examiners (TSBDE) under 22 TAC Chapter 108 requires dental offices administering local anesthesia to maintain a minimum emergency drug kit. The required items include epinephrine 1:1000 for anaphylaxis, diphenhydramine (Benadryl) for allergic reactions, nitroglycerin for angina, aspirin for suspected myocardial infarction, a bronchodilator (such as albuterol) for bronchospasm, and glucose or oral sugar source for hypoglycemia. Offices that provide moderate or deep sedation have additional requirements under a separate permit, including reversal agents such as flumazenil and naloxone. All emergency drugs must be within their labeled expiration dates and stored per manufacturer specifications — a quarterly audit of expiration dates is a best practice.

turns.user_message: One last facilities question — we want to repaint the waiting room. The building was built in 1987. Do we need a lead paint test before we start?
turns.assistant_message: Yes, for a commercial building constructed before 1978, EPA regulations under the Renovation, Repair, and Painting (RRP) Rule (40 CFR Part 745) require that a certified renovator test for lead-based paint or presume its presence and follow lead-safe work practices before disturbing painted surfaces. Your 1987 building was actually built after the 1978 cutoff year for the RRP Rule's presumption, so the rule technically doesn't apply to surfaces in buildings built after 1978. However, since your building was built in 1987 — after the cutoff — you're not required to test or follow RRP protocols for the waiting room repaint. That said, if you have any reason to believe non-standard or imported paints were used, a quick XRF or swab test before sanding is inexpensive and eliminates any doubt.

Counting 14 business days forward from February 14, 2025 — and excluding weekends — brings the end of the validation window to March 5, 2025. That means validation would be completed by March 5, 2025, which is two days after the March 3, 2025 go-live date, so the team should confirm with the Curve rep whether the clock starts on the decommission date itself or the following business day to avoid a conflict with go-live.
premise: a dentist's office replacing its appointment software
